name: Charles Rowoldt
bio: Charles Rowoldt was a Minneapolis worker, once secretary of the Hennepin County Workers Alliance, whom the government tried for two decades to deport to Germany because of his Depression-era political affiliations. In 1955 a fresh round of proceedings forced his case to the Circuit Court of Appeals; his fight reached the Supreme Court as Rowoldt v. Perfetto (1957).
charges: Deportation under the immigration laws — for past left-wing political affiliation
convicted: Two decades of deportation proceedings; renewed in 1955

name: Sang Ryun Park
bio: Sang Ryun Park was the English-language editor of the Los Angeles Korean-American paper Korean Independence, arrested for deportation to South Korea under the McCarran-Walter Act as part of the harassment of the anti-Syngman Rhee paper. A federal judge suspended the deportation order, rebuking the Immigration Service for 'summarily disposing of a man's life.'
charges: Deportation under the McCarran-Walter Act — to South Korea
convicted: Arrested for deportation; order suspended by a federal judge (1955)

name: John Juhn
bio: John Juhn was associated with the Los Angeles Korean-American paper Korean Independence and faced deportation to South Korea, where, as an opponent of the Syngman Rhee regime, supporters said he would face 'certain death.' His reopened deportation hearing was set for January 1956.
charges: Deportation under the immigration laws — to South Korea

name: Thomas Dutton
bio: Thomas Dutton was a 70-year-old Detroit carpenter and railwayman, in the United States about 46 years, ordered deported to England in 1955 on the testimony of two paid informers that he had attended Communist meetings around 1929. The deportation was temporarily stayed under public pressure.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran-Walter Act — on informers' claims of 1929 Communist meetings
sentence: Faced deportation to England after 46 years in the U.S.

name: Joel Doty
bio: Joel Doty was one of four Minnesota farm brothers — sons of William N. Doty of Bruno — who refused on conscientious grounds to cooperate with conscription. Having already served about two years in 1951–52 for refusing to register, he walked to jail again in March 1955 under a new two-year sentence for refusing induction.
charges: Refusing induction into the armed forces (Selective Service Act)

name: Orin Doty
bio: Orin Doty was one of the four conscientious-objector Doty brothers of Bruno, Minnesota, who refused to cooperate with the draft. After serving an earlier term for refusing to register, he was jailed again in March 1955 on a new two-year sentence for refusing induction.
charges: Refusing induction into the armed forces (Selective Service Act)

name: Paul Doty
bio: Paul Doty was one of the four Doty brothers of Bruno, Minnesota, conscientious objectors who refused to cooperate with conscription. After an earlier term for refusing to register, he was jailed again in March 1955 under a two-year sentence for refusing induction.
charges: Refusing induction into the armed forces (Selective Service Act)

name: Sid Doty
bio: Sid Doty was the youngest of the four conscientious-objector Doty brothers of Bruno, Minnesota, who refused to cooperate with the draft. Like his brothers, after an earlier term for refusing to register he was jailed again in March 1955 on a new two-year sentence for refusing induction.
charges: Refusing induction into the armed forces (Selective Service Act)

name: A. J. Muste
bio: The Rev. A. J. Muste, the dean of American pacifism, was one of about 29 pacifists arrested in New York City in June 1955 for refusing to take shelter during the 'Operation Alert' mock nuclear-attack drill — a conscientious protest against civil-defense preparations for atomic war. He was jailed on $1,500 bail and faced up to a year in prison under the State Defense Emergency Act.
charges: Violating the New York State Defense Emergency Act — refusing to take shelter in a civil-defense drill
sentence: Held on $1,500 bail; faced up to a year

name: Bayard Rustin
bio: Bayard Rustin, the Black pacifist and civil-rights strategist who would later organize the 1963 March on Washington, led members of the War Resisters League in refusing to take shelter during New York City's June 1955 'Operation Alert' civil-defense drill. He was among the roughly 29 arrested and jailed on $1,500 bail.
charges: Violating the New York State Defense Emergency Act — refusing to take shelter in a civil-defense drill
sentence: Held on $1,500 bail; faced up to a year

name: Walter Lee Irvin
bio: Walter Lee Irvin was one of the 'Groveland Four,' Black men accused of raping a white woman in Lake County, Florida in 1949 in a case the NAACP fought as a racial frame-up. After the Supreme Court ordered a new trial, Sheriff Willis McCall shot Irvin and killed co-defendant Samuel Shepherd while transporting them in 1951; re-convicted and sentenced to death, Irvin had his sentence commuted to life on December 15, 1955.
charges: Rape (capital) — a racial frame-up championed by the NAACP
convicted: Convicted; death sentence commuted to life December 1955

name: Sammie Ingram
bio: Sammie Ingram was a son of Rosa Lee Ingram, the Georgia sharecropper widow, convicted with his mother and brother Wallace in 1948 of murdering a white man the family said had attacked her — a case championed nationally as a racial frame-up of Black defendants who acted in self-defense. About 14 when sentenced to life, he was still imprisoned in 1955 when the parole board again denied release.
charges: Murder — a racial self-defense case championed as a frame-up

name: Joseph DeLaine
bio: The Rev. Joseph A. DeLaine was the AME minister who organized the Clarendon County, South Carolina school-desegregation petition that became part of Brown v. Board of Education. After his church was burned and nightriders fired on his home, he fired back and was charged with 'assault with intent to kill'; he fled the state, and New York's governor refused to extradite him on what supporters called a frame-up of a civil-rights leader.
charges: Assault with intent to kill — after firing back at nightriders; framed as political persecution
convicted: Indicted in South Carolina 1955; fought extradition from New York
